claim: Transport of biologically active molecules across tight epithelial barriers is a major challenge preventing therapeutic peptides from oral drug delivery.
source: Transport of biologically active molecules across tight epithelial barriers is a major challenge preventing therapeutic peptides from oral drug delivery.
evidence: This is a statement of a known problem in the field, drawing from established scientific understanding.

claim: Peptide cargoes covalently fused to glycosphingolipids with ceramide domains containing C6:0 or smaller fatty acids were transported with 20-100-fold greater efficiency across epithelial barriers in vitro and in vivo.
source: Peptide cargoes covalently fused to glycosphingolipids with ceramide domains containing C6:0 or smaller fatty acids were transported with 20-100-fold greater efficiency across epithelial barriers in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing transport efficiency measurements.

claim: The enhanced transport efficiency was explained by structure-function of the ceramide domain in intracellular sorting and by the affinity of the glycosphingolipid species for insertion into and retention in cell membranes.
source: This was explained by structure-function of the ceramide domain in intracellular sorting and by the affinity of the glycosphingolipid species for insertion into and retention in cell membranes.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on experimental observations and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In mice, GLP-1 fused to short-chain glycosphingolipids was rapidly and systemically absorbed after gastric gavage to affect glucose tolerance with serum bioavailability comparable to intraperitoneal injection of GLP-1 alone.
source: In mice, GLP-1 fused to short-chain glycosphingolipids was rapidly and systemically absorbed after gastric gavage to affect glucose tolerance with serum bioavailability comparable to intraperitoneal injection of GLP-1 alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experimental data from mouse studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: The pathway for absorption of large solutes across epithelial cells lining mucosal surfaces is by transcytosis.
source: In the case of epithelial cells lining mucosal surfaces, the pathway for absorption of large solutes is by transcytosis – a process of transcellular endosome trafficking that connects one surface of the cell with the other (Tuma and Hubbard, 2003; Mostov et al., 2000; Garcia-Castillo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous scientific literature.

claim: The structure of the ceramide (lipid) domain plays a decisive role in the intracellular trafficking of the glycosphingolipid GM1.
source: These studies were informed by our findings that the structure of the ceramide (lipid) domain plays a decisive role in the intracellular trafficking of the glycosphingolipid GM1, the lipid receptor responsible for cholera toxin entry into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) of host cells and required for disease (Chinnapen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: GM1 species containing ceramides with 'kinked' cis-unsaturated C18:1 or C16:1 fatty acids, or non-native 'short chain' C12:0 fatty acids, enter the sorting/recycling endosome of epithelial cells allowing for transport to various intracellular destinations.
source: GM1 species containing ceramides with 'kinked' cis-unsaturated C18:1 or C16:1 fatty acids, or non-native 'short chain' C12:0 fatty acids, enter the sorting/recycling endosome of epithelial cells allowing for transport to various intracellular destinations: including the recycling pathway and retrograde pathway to the Golgi and ER.
evidence: This claim is based on previous experimental observations by the authors.

claim: GM1 species with 'kinked' cis-unsaturated or short chain fatty acids do not efficiently traffic into the late endosome-lysosome pathway.
source: These lipids do not efficiently traffic into the late endosome-lysosome pathway.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from previous studies.

claim: GM1 sphingolipids with long saturated fatty acid chains (C16:0 or longer) sort almost exclusively into late endosomes and lysosomes.
source: In contrast, GM1 sphingolipids with long saturated fatty acid chains (C16:0 or longer) sort almost exclusively into late endosomes and lysosomes (Chinnapen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The sorting step separating the intracellular distributions of closely related lipids emerges from the early sorting endosome.
source: The sorting step separating the intracellular distributions of these closely related lipids emerges from the early sorting endosome, and we find it robust across all cell lines so far tested.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations across multiple cell lines.

claim: The lipid sorting observations are consistent with the two major models for lipid sorting: one by molecular shape and the other by membrane microdomains (lipid rafts).
source: Our observations are consistent with the two major models for lipid sorting: one by molecular shape (Hao et al., 2004; Mayor et al., 1993; Mukherjee et al., 1999) and the other by membrane microdomains (lipid rafts) (Brown, 2006; Simons and Ehehalt, 2002; Simons and Vaz, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established models in the literature.

claim: GM1 species with cis-unsaturated or short-chain fatty acids that efficiently enter the recycling endosome also sort into the transcytosis pathway in polarized epithelial cells.
source: The same GM1 species with cis-unsaturated or short-chain fatty acids that efficiently enter the recycling endosome also sort into this pathway (Saslowsky et al., 2013; te Welscher et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous attempts showed that glycosphingolipid species were capable of sorting a therapeutic cargo into the transcytotic pathway but release into solution to effect transport across epithelial barriers in vitro or absorption into the systemic circulation in vivo was not detectable.
source: Our first attempt to test this idea showed that these glycosphingolipid species were capable of sorting a therapeutic cargo into the transcytotic pathway. But release into solution to effect transport across epithelial barriers in vitro, or absorption into the systemic circulation in vivo was not detectable (te Welscher et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: A non-degradable all D-isomer reporter peptide was developed for structure-function studies on the ceramide domain.
source: To test if GM1 glycosphingolipids can be harnessed for biologic drug delivery, we first developed a non-degradable all D-isomer reporter peptide for structure-function studies on the ceramide domain.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach taken in the study.

claim: The reporter peptide was designed to contain two functional groups: a biotin for high-affinity streptavidin-enrichment and an alkyne reactive group for chemical ligation to fluorophore molecules and quantitative detection.
source: The reporter peptide was designed to contain two functional groups, a biotin for high-affinity streptavidin-enrichment, and an alkyne reactive group for chemical ligation to fluorophore molecules and quantitative detection.
evidence: This describes the design of the experimental tool used in the study.

claim: A C-terminal reactive aminooxy was used for coupling the reporter peptide to the oligosaccharide domain of the different GM1 species.
source: A C-terminal reactive aminooxy was used for coupling the reporter peptide to the oligosaccharide domain of the different GM1 species (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (te Welscher et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the chemical coupling method used, supported by figures and citation.

claim: The functional groups on the reporter peptide (biotin, alkyne, fluorophore and combinations) had no confounding effects on GM1 trafficking.
source: The functional groups on the reporter peptide, that is biotin, alkyne, fluorophore and combinations of, were tested to verify the absence of confounding effects on GM1 trafficking (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental validation shown in the figure.

claim: Peptide-coupled GM1 species containing cis-unsaturated or short fatty acid ceramide domains sorted into small cytoplasmic vesicles and basolateral membranes consistent with the recycling and transcytotic pathways.
source: In all cases, the peptide-coupled GM1 species containing cis-unsaturated or short fatty acid ceramide domains sorted into small cytoplasmic vesicles and basolateral membranes consistent with the recycling and transcytotic pathways, whereas the peptide-coupled GM1 species containing saturated long fatty acid ceramide domains did not; they were sorted into larger cytoplasmic puncta consistent with the late endosome/lysosome instead (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in the figure.

claim: Peptide-coupled GM1 species containing saturated long fatty acid ceramide domains were sorted into larger cytoplasmic puncta consistent with the late endosome/lysosome.
source: In all cases, the peptide-coupled GM1 species containing cis-unsaturated or short fatty acid ceramide domains sorted into small cytoplasmic vesicles and basolateral membranes consistent with the recycling and transcytotic pathways, whereas the peptide-coupled GM1 species containing saturated long fatty acid ceramide domains did not; they were sorted into larger cytoplasmic puncta consistent with the late endosome/lysosome instead (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in the figure.

claim: Both sorting events (recycling/transcytotic and lysosomal) were blocked at 4°C consistent with uptake by endocytosis.
source: Both events were blocked at 4°C consistent with uptake by endocytosis.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations at different temperatures.

claim: It is the structure of the fatty acid that dominates in the sorting reactions.
source: Thus, it is the structure of the fatty acid that dominates in the sorting reactions (Chinnapen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on experimental data and supported by citation.

claim: A quantitative assay for transcytosis was developed that is sensitive to picomolar concentrations and linear over a large 6-log dynamic range.
source: The assay is sensitive to picomolar concentrations and linear over a large 6-log dynamic range (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the assay developed, supported by data in the figure.

claim: GM1-peptide fusion molecules containing ceramide domains with C6:0, C4:0, C2:0 fatty acids or lyso-GM1 showed approximately a 10-fold increase in transepithelial transport compared to controls when tested on human intestinal T84 cell monolayers.
source: When tested on human intestinal T84 cell monolayers, we found approximately a 10-fold increase in transepithelial transport (PAPP) for the GM1 ceramide species containing C6:0, C4:0, C2:0, fatty acids or lyso-GM1 as compared to controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the transcytosis assay.

claim: Introduction of an unsaturated cis-double bond to the short chain ceramide fatty acids (C12:1 and C6:1) had no effect on transcytosis in comparison to the saturated species (C12:0 and C6:0).
source: Introduction of an unsaturated cis-double bond to the short chain ceramide fatty acids (C12:1 and C6:1) had no effect on transcytosis in comparison to the saturated species (C12:0 and C6:0) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The effect of the cis-double bond on short chain fatty acids contrasts with the dramatic effect the cis-double bond induces in trafficking of the long fatty-acid chain GM1 glycosphingolipids.
source: This result is in contrast to the dramatic effect the cis-double bond induces in trafficking of the long fatty-acid chain GM1 glycosphingolipids (Chinnapen et al., 2012; Saslowsky et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Transepithelial transport was dose-dependent for the C6:0-GM1-peptide fusion and greatly exceeded transport of the unconjugated reporter peptide over a wide range of concentrations.
source: Transepithelial transport was dose-dependent for the C6:0-GM1-peptide fusion (grey bars) and greatly exceeded transport of the unconjugated reporter peptide (white bars) over a wide range of concentrations (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Transcellular transport of the peptide cargo was dependent on fusion to the GM1 glycosphingolipid.
source: Mixing experiments using unconjugated GM1 and reporter peptide as individual molecules confirmed that transcellular transport of the peptide cargo was dependent on fusion to the GM1 glycosphingolipid (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mixing experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Neither the unfused reporter peptide nor the GM1-peptide fusion had any detectable confounding effects on cell viability as determined by MTT assay.
source: Neither the unfused reporter peptide nor the GM1-peptide fusion had any detectable confounding effects on cell viability as determined by measurement of metabolic activity (MTT assay), or monolayer integrity and tight junction function assessed as trans-epithelial resistance (TEER) or dextran flux (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in the figure.

claim: Neither the unfused reporter peptide nor the GM1-peptide fusion had any detectable confounding effects on monolayer integrity and tight junction function assessed as trans-epithelial resistance (TEER) or dextran flux.
source: Neither the unfused reporter peptide nor the GM1-peptide fusion had any detectable confounding effects on cell viability as determined by measurement of metabolic activity (MTT assay), or monolayer integrity and tight junction function assessed as trans-epithelial resistance (TEER) or dextran flux (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEER and dextran flux measurements shown in the figure.

claim: No detectable transport of GM1-peptide fusions across T84 cell monolayers occurred at 4°C, consistent with transport via transcytosis.
source: We found no detectable transport of GM1-peptide fusions across T84 cell monolayers at 4°C, consistent with transport via transcytosis (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by temperature-dependent transport data shown in the figure.

claim: The C6:0-GM1-peptide fusion localized to basolateral membranes in cells chased at 37°C, but not at 10°C.
source: We found the C6:0-GM1-peptide fusion localized to basolateral membranes in cells chased at 37°C, but not at 10°C (Figure 2B; left and middle panels respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by live cell confocal microscopy data shown in the figure.

claim: After breaking open tight junctions by removal of extracellular Ca2+ (EDTA treatment), the GM1-peptide fusion molecule gained access to the basolateral membrane at 10°C.
source: Only after breaking open tight junctions by removal of extracellular Ca2+ (EDTA treatment) did the GM1-peptide fusion molecule gain access to the basolateral membrane at 10°C (Figure 2B, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with EDTA treatment shown in the figure.

claim: For the C6:0 and C12:0 GM1-peptide fusion molecules, transport into the basolateral reservoir was strongly inhibited by Dyngo-4A treatment, consistent with active transcellular transport by transcytosis.
source: For the C6:0 and C12:0 GM1-peptide fusion molecules, transport into the basolateral reservoir was strongly inhibited by Dyngo-4A treatment, consistent with active transcellular transport by transcytosis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamin inhibition experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Dyngo-4A had no detectable effect on transport of the reporter peptide alone, as expected for diffusion of solutes by paracellular leak.
source: In contrast, Dyngo-4A had no detectable effect on transport of the reporter peptide alone, as expected for diffusion of solutes by paracellular leak.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and is consistent with expected behavior for paracellular transport.

claim: The exocyst complex is necessary for efficient receptor-mediated transcytosis of immunoglobulins.
source: The exocyst complex is necessary for efficient receptor-mediated transcytosis of immunoglobulins (Oztan et al., 2007; Nelms et al., 2017), and esiRNA knock-down of EXOC2 subunit caused the predicted 50% decrease in trans-epithelial transport of the C6:0-GM1 peptide fusion molecule (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: esiRNA knock-down of EXOC2 subunit caused a 50% decrease in trans-epithelial transport of the C6:0-GM1 peptide fusion molecule.
source: The exocyst complex is necessary for efficient receptor-mediated transcytosis of immunoglobulins (Oztan et al., 2007; Nelms et al., 2017), and esiRNA knock-down of EXOC2 subunit caused the predicted 50% decrease in trans-epithelial transport of the C6:0-GM1 peptide fusion molecule (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic knockdown experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Transport of the unfused reporter peptide was not affected by exocyst knockdown.
source: In contrast, transport of the unfused reporter peptide was not affected by exocyst KD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the knockdown experiments.

claim: Fusion of a peptide cargo to certain GM1 species enables active transport of the peptide across the epithelial barrier by transcytosis.
source: Thus, fusion of a peptide cargo to certain GM1 species enables active transport of the peptide across the epithelial barrier by transcytosis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental approaches presented.

claim: There was no detectable difference between C12:0 and C6:0-GM1-peptide fusions in the rate of transcytosis measured by pulse chase.
source: By this method, we found no detectable difference among the two GM1 species in the rate of transcytosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulse-chase experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Monolayers loaded with the C12:0-GM1 peptide fusion stained brightly at both the apical and basolateral membranes after longer chase times.
source: Monolayers loaded with the C12:0-GM1 peptide fusion stained brightly at both the apical (bottom left panel) and basolateral membranes (bottom right panel).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments.

claim: Monolayers loaded with the C6:0-GM1 peptide fusion showed no fluorescence after longer chase times.
source: In stark contrast, monolayers loaded with the C6:0-GM1 peptide fusion showed no fluorescence (middle panels).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments.

claim: The C6:0-GM1 fusion molecule showed a faster and more complete diffusion from membrane to solution compared to the longer chain C12:0-GM1-peptide.
source: Results show a faster and more complete diffusion from membrane to solution for the C6:0-GM1 fusion molecule (Figure 3B and C; red curve) compared to the longer chain C12:0-GM1-peptide (blue curve).
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane release kinetics data shown in the figures.

claim: Faster and more complete release into solution was also observed for the C2:0-GM1-peptide fusion molecule.
source: Faster and more complete release into solution was also observed for the C2:0-GM1-peptide fusion molecule (Figure 3B and C; purple curve).
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane release kinetics data shown in the figures.

claim: The greater efficiency for transepithelial transport by the short chain GM1 species is largely explained by their greater efficiency of diffusion from membrane to solution after transcytosis.
source: Thus, the greater efficiency for transepithelial transport by the short chain GM1 species is largely explained by their greater efficiency of diffusion from membrane to solution after transcytosis.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the membrane release kinetics data.

claim: The oligosaccharide head group of glycosphingolipids acts to trap sphingolipids in the outer leaflet of cell membranes, rendering the lipids dependent on membrane trafficking for their distribution across the cell.
source: In all cases, however, the oligosaccharide head group acts to trap sphingolipids in the outer leaflet of cell membranes, thus rendering the lipids dependent on membrane trafficking for their distribution across the cell.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of glycosphingolipid biology.

claim: The GM3-C12:0-peptide fusion molecule crosses epithelial monolayers far more efficiently than the closely related GM1-C12:0-peptide, and as efficiently as the GM1-C6:0 and C2:0 species.
source: When tested for transcytosis, we unexpectedly found that the GM3-C12:0-peptide fusion molecule crosses epithelial monolayers far more efficiently that the closely related GM1-C12:0-peptide; and as efficiently as the GM1-C6:0 and C2:0 species (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcytosis assay data shown in the figure.

claim: Transepithelial transport for the GM3-C6:0-peptide was approximately 2-fold greater than that observed for the GM1-C6:0-peptide when compared directly.
source: Similarly, transepithelial transport for the GM3-C6:0-peptide was approximately 2-fold greater than that observed for the GM1-C6:0-peptide when compared directly (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative transcytosis data shown in the figure.

claim: Transport of GM3-C12:0-peptide fusion was strongly inhibited by pretreatment with the dynamin inhibitor Dyngo-4A, implicating active transcellular trafficking by transcytosis.
source: Transport was strongly inhibited by pretreatment with the dynamin inhibitor Dyngo-4A, implicating active transcellular trafficking by transcytosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by dynamin inhibition experiments.

claim: The C12:0-GM3-peptide fusion showed a higher rate of release to solution compared to the GM1 fusion molecule.
source: In membrane-release studies, we found a higher rate of release to solution for the C12:0-GM3-peptide fusion (green curve) when compared to the GM1 fusion molecule (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by membrane release kinetics data shown in the figures.

claim: The GM1 glycosphingolipid species appear to be retained in the membrane more tightly than the GM3 species containing the same ceramide domains.
source: Thus, the GM1 glycosphingolipid species appear to be retained in the membrane more tightly than the GM3 species containing the same ceramide domains.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparative membrane release data.

claim: GM1 lipids might be further tethered to the membrane by a form of lectin-binding at the cell surface.
source: Because GM3 lacks a free terminal galactose, we hypothesized the GM1 lipids, which contain the terminal galactose, might be further tethered to the membrane by a form of lectin-binding at the cell surface.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed differences between GM1 and GM3.

claim: Enhanced release of C12:0-GM1 from the membrane occurred in the presence of excess free lactose, but not excess mannitol, implicating interaction with a galactose-specific lectin membrane tether.
source: These studies show enhanced release from the membrane in the presence of excess free lactose, but not excess mannitol, implicating interaction with a galactose-specific lectin membrane tether (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive inhibition experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Lactose at high 100 mM concentrations competed both the GM1 and GM3 species off the membrane.
source: Here we find that lactose at high 100 mM concentrations competed both the GM1 and GM3 species off the membrane (not shown) but at lower doses (5 mM) lactose released only the GM1-fusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-dependent competition experiments.

claim: At lower doses (5 mM), lactose released only the GM1-fusion but not GM3-fusion.
source: Here we find that lactose at high 100 mM concentrations competed both the GM1 and GM3 species off the membrane (not shown) but at lower doses (5 mM) lactose released only the GM1-fusion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-dependent competition experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Gal-GalNAc (5 mM) was effective at enhancing release of only the GM1-fusion molecules.
source: Likewise, Gal-GalNAc (5 mM) was effective at enhancing release of only the GM1-fusion molecules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by competitive inhibition experiments shown in the figure.

claim: The oligosaccharide domain of the glycosphingolipids can affect the efficiency of transport across epithelial barriers by interacting with lectin-like molecules at the cell surface.
source: Thus, the oligosaccharide domain of the glycosphingolipids can also affect the efficiency of transport across epithelial barriers, we propose by interacting with lectin-like molecules at the cell surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the competitive inhibition experiments with sugars.

claim: Nearly 3% of the applied dose of C4:0-GM1-peptide fusion was absorbed into the systemic circulation at 15 and 30 min after intragastric gavage to mice.
source: At both time points, we find evidence of absorption into the systemic circulation for the GM1-peptide fusion molecules (nearly 3% of the applied dose), but not for the unfused peptide (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo absorption data shown in the figure.

claim: The unfused peptide was not detectably absorbed into the systemic circulation after intragastric gavage to mice.
source: At both time points, we find evidence of absorption into the systemic circulation for the GM1-peptide fusion molecules (nearly 3% of the applied dose), but not for the unfused peptide (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo absorption data shown in the figure.

claim: The C12:0-GM3-peptide fusion molecule was absorbed into the systemic circulation after gastric gavage.
source: The same results were obtained for the C12:0-GM3-peptide fusion molecule (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo absorption data shown in the figure.

claim: At 1 hr after gastric gavage, the glycosphingolipid-peptide fusion molecule was found in the liver, but not the unfused peptide.
source: We also measured uptake into the liver, where at 1 hr after gastric gavage we find the glycosphingolipid-peptide fusion molecule, but not the unfused peptide (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by tissue distribution data shown in the figure.

claim: Fusion to the glycosphingolipids facilitated absorption of the peptide cargo across the intestine and into blood and liver.
source: Thus, fusion to the glycosphingolipids facilitated absorption of the peptide cargo across the intestine and into the two tissues we sampled, blood and liver.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the in vivo absorption and distribution data.

claim: The C6:0-GM1-peptide could be visualized by two-photon microscopy within the epithelial barrier in all regions of the nasal epithelium after topical nasal administration.
source: In this case, the C6:0-GM1-peptide (green labeling; Figure 4D) could be visualized by two-photon microscopy within the epithelial barrier in all regions of the nasal epithelium (Figure 4D), including in areas of pseudostratified (top right panels) and simple columnar epithelial tissues (bottom right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-photon microscopy imaging data shown in the figure.

claim: Uptake of the unfused peptide in nasal epithelium was very rarely detected after topical nasal administration.
source: Uptake of the unfused peptide, applied at the same dose, was very rarely detected (left panels).
evidence: This is an observation from two-photon microscopy experiments.

claim: Approximately a 10-fold increase in blood levels was found for the GM1-peptide fusion molecules 15 min after nasal administration, compared to peptide alone.
source: Here, we find approximately a 10-fold increase in blood levels for the GM1-peptide fusion molecules, compared to peptide alone (which is close to background).
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical analysis of blood samples.

claim: Efficient absorption of the C12:0-GM1-peptide fusion molecules was found in the nasal epithelium, similar to results with the C12:0-GM3-peptide species in the intestine.
source: Unexpectedly, in the nasal epithelium, we find evidence for efficient absorption of the C12:0-GM1-peptide fusion molecules, similar to our results with the C12:0-GM3-peptide species in the intestine.
evidence: This is an observation from in vivo experiments comparing different tissues.

claim: Different tissues may interact in different ways with the oligosaccharide domains of glycosphingolipids.
source: The result suggests that different tissues may interact in different ways with the oligosaccharide domains of glycosphingolipids.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the tissue-specific differences observed.

claim: The nasal epithelium may not bind the GM1 oligosaccharide, thus allowing for more efficient release from cell membranes into solution after transcytosis and systemic absorption.
source: In this case, the nasal epithelium may not bind the GM1 oligosaccharide, thus allowing for more efficient release from cell membranes into solution after transcytosis and systemic absorption.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed tissue-specific differences.

claim: GLP-1 and related peptides have become important drugs in the management of type two diabetes mellitus, by both promoting weight reduction and sensitizing glucose-stimulated insulin release.
source: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and related peptides have become important drugs in the management of type two diabetes mellitus, by both promoting weight reduction and sensitizing glucose-stimulated insulin release (van Bloemendaal et al., 2014; Heppner and Perez-Tilve, 2015; Tran et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: A major factor limiting the clinical utility of GLP-1 in many individuals is that all currently available preparations must be delivered by subcutaneous injection.
source: A major factor limiting the clinical utility in many individuals is the fact that all currently available preparations must be delivered by subcutaneous injection.
evidence: This is a statement about current clinical practice and limitations.

claim: The fusion of C6:0-GM1 to GLP-1 caused some loss of function, but the molecule remained highly potent as an incretin hormone, closely comparable to that of the controls.
source: The fusion of C6:0-GM1 to GLP-1 caused some loss of function, but the molecule remained highly potent as an incretin hormone, closely comparable to that of the controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by bioactivity assay data.

claim: An even greater effect of the glycosphingolipids on transepithelial GLP-1 transport (20–100-fold above controls) was found compared to the reporter peptide.
source: Here, we find an even greater effect of the glycosphingolipids on transepithelial GLP-1 transport (20–100-fold above controls).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcytosis assay data for GLP-1.

claim: The greater effect on GLP-1 transport is explained by a much lower rate of paracellular leak for the larger sized 40-residue GLP-1 peptide.
source: This is explained by a much lower rate of paracellular leak for the larger sized 40-residue GLP-1 peptide.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on size-exclusion principles.

claim: Size-exclusion from tight junctions is a well-known determinant of paracellular solute diffusion across intact epithelial barriers.
source: Such size-exclusion from tight junctions is a well-known determinant of paracellular solute diffusion across intact epithelial barriers.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in epithelial biology.

claim: A lower peak and more rapid return of blood glucose to normal levels was found in animals gavaged the C6:0-GM1-GLP-1 fusion molecules compared to animals gavaged GLP-1 peptide.
source: Here, we find a lower peak and more rapid return of blood glucose to normal levels in the animals gavaged the C6:0-GM1-GLP-1 fusion molecules compared to animals gavaged GLP-1 peptide (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in the figures.

claim: The effect on glucose tolerance by gastrically administered C6:0-GM1-GLP-1 was similar to the effect achieved by the intraperitoneal injection of GLP-1 peptide alone, implicating an equally high level of bioavailability for the gastrically-delivered GM1-fusion molecule.
source: The effect on glucose tolerance by gastrically administered C6:0-GM1-GLP-1 was similar to the effect achieved by the intraperitoneal injection of GLP-1 peptide alone, implicating an equally high level of bioavailability for the gastrically-delivered GM1-fusion molecule (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative glucose tolerance test data shown in the figure.

claim: Absorption of the GM1-GLP-1 fusion molecule into the blood was confirmed, but not for unfused GLP-1, by measuring GLP-1 activity in blood samples by streptavidin capture and quantitative luciferase bioassay.
source: First, we measured GLP-1 activity in blood samples by streptavidin capture and quantitative luciferase bioassay (Figure 5E). The results show absorption of the GM1-GLP-1 fusion molecule into the blood, but not for unfused GLP-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by bioassay data from blood samples shown in the figure.

claim: Evidence for absorption of the GLP-1 cargo when fused to the C6:0-GM1 transport vehicle was found, but no absorption for the unfused GLP-1 peptide, using an all D-amino acid isomer of GLP-1 coupled to AF488.
source: Again, we find evidence for absorption of the GLP-1 cargo when fused to the C6:0-GM1 transport vehicle, but no absorption for the unfused GLP-1 peptide (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by direct measurement of the D-isomer in blood shown in the figure.

claim: The efficiency of intestinal absorption enabled by fusion to C6:0-GM1 was almost as efficient as for IP injection of the peptide alone, implicating a high level of bioavailability for the GM1-fusion molecules applied by gastric gavage.
source: In all assays (Figure 5C–5F), we find the efficiency of intestinal absorption enabled by fusion to C6:0-GM1 was again almost as efficient as for IP injection of the peptide alone, implicating a high level of bioavailability for the GM1-fusion molecules applied by gastric gavage.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple assays shown in the figures.

claim: The C2:0-GM1-GLP-1 fusion molecule had no effect on glucose tolerance and was not detectably absorbed after gastric gavage.
source: Notably, however, the C2:0-GM1-GLP-1 fusion molecule had no effect on glucose tolerance (Figure 5D) and was not detectably absorbed after gastric gavage (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), even though this molecule was readily transported across epithelial monolayers in vitro (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance test and absorption data shown in the figures.

claim: The lack of in vivo absorption of C2:0-GM1-GLP-1 may be explained by lower affinity of the C2:0- (and lyso-) ceramide domains for incorporation into cell membranes.
source: This may be explained by lower affinity of the C2:0- (and lyso-) ceramide domains for incorporation into cell membranes, as inferred from membrane loading and release assays (Figure 3B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on membrane loading and release data shown in the figures.

claim: The difference in biology (transcytosis in vitro versus absorption in vivo) becomes apparent only in vivo where the conditions for epithelial uptake and transport are not optimized as they are in vitro.
source: The difference in biology (transcytosis in vitro versus absorption in vivo) becomes apparent only in vivo where the conditions for epithelial uptake and transport are not optimized as they are in vitro.
evidence: This is an interpretation explaining the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: Further shortening of the fatty acid beyond C4:0 did not amplify transepithelial transport and clinical utility as initially expected.
source: Thus, although it seemed at first glance that further shortening of the fatty acid beyond C4:0 should amplify transepithelial transport and thus clinical utility, this was not the case and the result informs further development of the technology.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the unexpected results with C2:0-GM1.

claim: Fusion of therapeutic peptides to GM1 and GM3 glycosphingolipids with short fatty acids enables their active transport across tight epithelial barriers by transcytosis.
source: In summary, we find that fusion of therapeutic peptides to GM1 and GM3 glycosphingolipids with short fatty acids enables their active transport across tight epithelial barriers by transcytosis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: Fusion of GLP-1 to the lipid carriers allows for gastric (oral) absorption with high bioavailability and the expected effects on blood glucose.
source: In the case of the incretin hormone GLP-1, fusion to the lipid carriers allows for gastric (oral) absorption with high bioavailability and the expected effects on blood glucose, highlighting the potential use of this technology in clinical applications.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the GLP-1 experimental data.

claim: The findings delineate a novel synthetic method for enabling absorption of therapeutic peptides across mucosal surfaces in vivo.
source: Our findings delineate a novel synthetic method for enabling absorption of therapeutic peptides across mucosal surfaces in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main contribution of the work.

claim: The approach is based on the natural biology of lipid sorting for the glycosphingolipids, which depends primarily on the structure of the ceramide domain to allow for trafficking in the transcytotic pathway.
source: The approach is based on the natural biology of lipid sorting for the glycosphingolipids, which depends primarily on the structure of the ceramide domain to allow for trafficking in the transcytotic pathway, and thus active transport across mucosal surfaces without barrier disruption.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanistic basis of the technology.

claim: For applications requiring systemic drug delivery, non-native glycosphingolipid carriers with ceramide domains containing short-chain fatty acids are required to allow for efficient release from cell membranes into the circulation after transcytosis.
source: For applications requiring systemic drug delivery, non-native glycosphingolipid carriers with ceramide domains containing short-chain fatty acids are required to allow for efficient release from cell membranes into the circulation after transcytosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the design requirements for the technology.

claim: The apparent high level of intestinal bioavailability enabled by the glycosphingolipid carriers is unprecedented.
source: The apparent high level of intestinal bioavailability enabled by the glycosphingolipid carriers is unprecedented.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the results.

claim: The mechanism(s) for transcellular trafficking co-opted by the cis-unsaturated or short chain fatty acid glycosphingolipids are not fully understood.
source: The mechanism(s) for transcellular trafficking co-opted by the cis-unsaturated or short chain fatty acid glycosphingolipids are not fully understood.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations in mechanistic understanding.

claim: The most robust sorting event for GM1 glycosphingolipids appears to occur in the early endosome where long saturated chain ceramides are trafficked to the late endosome/lysosome, and the cis-unsaturated and short-chain glycoceramides are not.
source: The most robust sorting event for GM1 glycosphingolipids appears to occur in the early endosome where long saturated chain ceramides are trafficked to the late endosome/lysosome, and the cis-unsaturated and short-chain glycoceramides are not ([Chinnapen et al., 2012] and Schmieder and Lencer unpublished results).
evidence: This claim is supported by published and unpublished data.

claim: It is possible the unsaturated and short-chain ceramide domains engage sorting mechanisms that dictate their trafficking to the recycling endosome and elsewhere.
source: It is possible the unsaturated and short-chain ceramide domains engage sorting mechanisms that dictate their trafficking to the recycling endosome and elsewhere, but we suggest it also possible that their trafficking might be stochastic after escape from the lysosomal pathway, essentially tracking along with bulk membrane flow.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claim: The trafficking of unsaturated and short-chain ceramide domains might be stochastic after escape from the lysosomal pathway, essentially tracking along with bulk membrane flow.
source: It is possible the unsaturated and short-chain ceramide domains engage sorting mechanisms that dictate their trafficking to the recycling endosome and elsewhere, but we suggest it also possible that their trafficking might be stochastic after escape from the lysosomal pathway, essentially tracking along with bulk membrane flow.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the observed trafficking patterns.

claim: The robust sorting event may occur only for the long chain saturated glycosphingolipids, directing them to the lysosome.
source: In other words, the robust sorting event may occur only for the long chain saturated glycosphingolipids, directing them to the lysosome.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the sorting mechanism.

claim: The oligosaccharide head group is a key structural feature enabling this technology because it traps the ceramide lipid in the outer membrane leaflet, preventing flip-flop between leaflets and rendering the molecule dependent on membrane dynamics for movement throughout the cell.
source: Another key structural feature enabling this technology must be the oligosaccharide head group. This domain traps the ceramide lipid in the outer membrane leaflet, preventing flip-flop between leaflets and thus rendering the molecule dependent on membrane dynamics for movement throughout the cell – an essential feature for a trafficking vehicle.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on known properties of glycosphingolipids.

claim: One way the extracellular oligosaccharide may affect the efficiency of transepithelial transport is by binding to adjacent membrane lectins, thus enhancing the tethering of the lipid to the membrane surface.
source: One way, we suggest, may be by binding to adjacent membrane lectins, thus enhancing the tethering of the lipid to the membrane surface.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental observations with GM1 and GM3.

claim: Differences have been reported between GM1 and GM3 with respect to plasma membrane localization and bilayer/curvature dynamics in vitro.
source: Differences have also been reported between GM1 and GM3 with respect to plasma membrane localization and bilayer/curvature dynamics in vitro (Cantù et al., 2011; Janich and Corbeil, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: One application for the glycosphingolipids would be as vehicles for systemic delivery of peptide hormones.
source: One would be as vehicles for systemic delivery of peptide hormones as demonstrated here, or for topical delivery of agonist or antagonist peptides to specific mucosal surfaces.
evidence: This is a proposed application based on the demonstrated results.

claim: Another application would be for topical delivery of agonist or antagonist peptides to specific mucosal surfaces.
source: One would be as vehicles for systemic delivery of peptide hormones as demonstrated here, or for topical delivery of agonist or antagonist peptides to specific mucosal surfaces.
evidence: This is a proposed application based on the demonstrated results.

claim: Another application would be for delivery of antigens or adjuvants to enable mucosal vaccination or oral tolerance.
source: Another would be for delivery of antigens or adjuvants to enable mucosal vaccination or oral tolerance.
evidence: This is a proposed application based on the demonstrated transport capabilities.

claim: It is possible that these glycosphingolipids will transport therapeutic proteins in the same way.
source: It is possible that these glycosphingolipids will transport therapeutic proteins in the same way.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: At least some of the basic principles for lipid sorting in epithelial cells will apply to endothelial cells.
source: Finally, while the biology of endosomes in endothelial cells is much less well understood, we believe at least some of the basic principles for lipid sorting in epithelial cells will apply to this cell type; and the glycosphingolipid carriers defined here may also be used to enable transport of biologics across tight endothelial barriers.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: The glycosphingolipid carriers defined here may be used to enable transport of biologics across tight endothelial barriers.
source: Finally, while the biology of endosomes in endothelial cells is much less well understood, we believe at least some of the basic principles for lipid sorting in epithelial cells will apply to this cell type; and the glycosphingolipid carriers defined here may also be used to enable transport of biologics across tight endothelial barriers.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

source: T84 cells were cultured in a 1:1 mixture of Ham's F12 medium and Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium with 2.5 mM L-glutamine, 95%; fetal bovine serum, 5%.

source: MDCK cells were maintained in DMEM supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated FBS and penicillin and streptomycin, all obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific.
evidence: This describes the cell culture methods used in the study.

source: T84 and MDCK cells were routinely confirmed to be negative for mycoplasma using a PCR kit from MD Biosciences.
evidence: This describes quality control measures for the cell lines used.
